items.question: How do you see Plato’s Timaeus as an inspiration for your approach to understanding deep learning systems?
items.object: Plato’s Timaeus as an inspiration for Timaeus’ approach to AI safety
items.answer: I think the story starts 2,500 years ago with Plato. Timaeus is a dialogue by Plato in which he puts forth sort of the first theory of everything. So it's a protochemistry where the elements—earth, wind, fire—are associated with Platonic forms, right? The cube and the icosahedron and the dodecahedron and these kinds of things. Now, the theory is completely wrong, but it's the first instance of somebody thinking, 'Hey, mathematics really has a chance of understanding the natural world,' and so it's that spirit that drives us today. Maybe we can find ideas in mathematics and the sciences that actually help us understand this new phase of matter, these deep learning systems, to help us make sure that they're safe. Also, in the Timaeus, the world is intelligent. So actually, the history of the universe is just a learning process, and physics is just a subset of learning theory.

Now, the theory is completely wrong, but it's the first instance of somebody thinking, 'Hey, mathematics really has a chance of understanding the natural world,' and so it's that spirit that drives us today. Maybe we can find ideas in mathematics and the sciences that actually help us understand this new phase of matter, these deep learning systems, to help us make sure that they're safe.
Also, in the Timaeus, the world is intelligent. So actually, the history of the universe is just a learning process, and physics is just a subset of learning theory.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between physics and learning theory that you invoked through Plato’s Timaeus?
items.object: The relationship between physics and learning theory
items.answer: I was mostly trying to troll your physicist listeners with that. I don't want to take a position on the kind of mathematical nature of reality. That seems like a bit of a tangent. But I mentioned that aspect of the Timaeus not completely idly, because there are a lot of deep connections between physics and learning theory, and those are some of the connections that inspire a lot of the work we do, particularly with statistical physics and so on. The study of learning machines is as deep as physics in many ways, and it's not a surprise that a lot of physicists are starting to devote their professional careers to understanding aspects of these systems.

items.question: What drew you, as an algebraic geometer, to Sumi Watanabe's singular learning theory as an approach to understanding deep learning?
items.object: Sumi Watanabe's singular learning theory
items.answer: At some point I was following the developments in deep learning, and they were very interesting, but it was completely separate from my professional life until I encountered Sumi Watanabe's work. He's a Japanese mathematician, the inventor of singular learning theory. It seems kind of hard to believe, but one of the core tenets of his work is that one of the very deep parts of algebraic geometry is central to Bayesian statistics. That was kind of curious to me, and I was also aware that people were not completely satisfied with the theoretical treatments of deep learning that existed at the time. So it seemed tempting to me as an algebraic geometer to adopt this language and approach to try and understand these systems. That's how I got into singular learning theory. That was a few years before I was drawn into thinking about AI safety. It was through the fundamental theory of Bayesian statistics. All parts of mathematics are ultimately connected at some level, right? So it's not necessarily super surprising that geometry comes into learning theory. There are other ways it enters, but that's one of them.

items.question: How do you think developmental interpretability can make understanding large neural networks more manageable?
items.object: Developmental interpretability
items.answer: All the research we're doing is based on singular learning theory, SLT. If I had to reduce that into one sentence, maybe the core idea of SLT is that the geometry of the loss landscape—the surface that we walk down when we're defining some sort of optimization process—contains important information for understanding neural networks and potentially steering them more reliably. This has applications, on the one hand, for interpretability and, on the other hand, for alignment. When we started looking into applications of this theory, which was at the time still very mathematical and theoretical, for empirically understanding neural networks two years ago, one of the first applications we came up with was this agenda we called developmental interpretability. Can you use SLT to better understand how neural networks develop over the course of training? The hope here is that development is an axis that can reduce the problem of interpretability to something more manageable. At the end of the day, all interpretability techniques are hoping that we can reduce the problem of understanding some 100-billion- or trillion-parameter model into fewer numbers, into something a little more manageable. One way you could try to do this is understand the changes that give rise to that model over the course of training. If there's a finite number of changes and the number of changes is much smaller than the number of parameters, then you've got a useful simplification for the model. That's what motivated developmental interpretability, or Dev, when we started two years ago.

items.question: Why do you consider two-dimensional pictures of neural-network loss landscapes misleading for understanding generalization?
items.object: Two-dimensional visualizations of neural-network loss landscapes
items.answer: To go back to algebraic geometry briefly: in two, one, or three dimensions, you can use pictures and intuition from pictures. But once you go to higher dimensions, your intuitions are not a reliable guide to how to think about these objects. That's where you try to bake your intuitions in lower dimensions into mathematical forms which continue to work, and that's in some sense what geometry is. I think these pictures of a two-dimensional surface of a loss landscape: the way you do that is by choosing two directions in a very high-dimensional space, taking that little plane, and plotting the loss as a function of the coordinates on that plane. One thing you're going to do with probability one if you choose a random slice like that is not see, for example, the degeneracy that determines generalization according to singular learning theory. In some sense, those pictures are maximally misleading when it comes to generalization. I'm not saying they're not useful, and they're certainly pretty, but in many cases the actual relevant geometry looks more like a bunch of planes intersecting in some kind of crazy way. That's what the level sets look like. If you take a valley in a loss landscape, the level sets—points at a given height above the floor, a given loss—will be like the edges of the valleys and will have some nice smooth shape. If you go to the very bottom of the valley, you'll eventually just get a single point. That's not what the level sets of loss landscapes look like. They're not smooth shapes like that. They're very complex geometric forms with lots of intersecting lines, lots of high-dimensional things that are kind of nilled up in various ways. Those are the singularities we're interested in.

items.question: What distinction do you draw between population loss and empirical loss when explaining the geometry that governs generalization?
items.object: Population loss versus empirical loss in understanding generalization
items.answer: To be clear, the loss landscape here means the population loss. This is a theoretical object. That's an important, subtle, and difficult point: you never actually have access to this object, the population loss. That would be if you could average over every sample from the true generating process. Say that was images; you could somehow average the loss over every possible draw from that data distribution. Of course, you never see that. If you're plotting an empirical loss landscape, you have some samples and compute the loss based on that. The actual geometry that dictates generalization mathematically is the geometry of the population loss, and that influences the behavior of all these empirical losses based on samples, but you never actually have access to that.

items.question: How do you establish that degeneracies in neural-network loss landscapes really exist when the population loss is normally inaccessible?
items.object: Evidence for degeneracies in neural-network loss landscapes
items.answer:
There's a few ways into that. One is to study very, very simple neural networks where you can actually figure out the population loss in closed form, and that's where Watanabe started. This was decades ago. He was studying tanh networks rather than modern neural networks, but you can take one-hidden-layer tanh networks, for instance, for a synthetic data distribution you can understand, write down the integrals, figure out what the population loss is, and study these degeneracies and see that they're real. They don't have any interesting relation to the data because the data isn't interesting; for interesting data, you can't actually do that calculation. But in these very synthetic settings, you can show what the degeneracies are, do various calculations, and study the theorems which connect generalization to geometry explicitly in examples. There are numerous examples, including full neural networks, albeit simple ones.

You can do things a bit more related to current practice. One of the papers we wrote looked at Anthropic's work on the toy model of superposition. There's an actual small autoencoder, and you can do the integrals there as well, write down and get the actual population loss, and study its geometry. We computed these degeneracies, and you can see that the training process is governed by these degeneracies in the way the theory says. Again, that's not a super interesting data distribution, and the degeneracies are complicated, but that's a case where you can find out what the degeneracies are.

items.question: How do you assess the significance of seemingly trivial degeneracies such as scaling symmetries in neural networks?
items.object: Scaling symmetries as neural-network degeneracies
items.answer:
There's a boring kind of degeneracy, which maybe it's worth getting out of the way: scaling symmetries and so on. If you have a ReLU, you can scale up the input and down the output by any positive real number. That's a way of changing the weights that doesn't change the function computed. You have a lot of degeneracies like that. Anytime you have two matrices being multiplied inside a network, like in attention, where the query and key matrices are multiplied, or various other matrices are multiplied, you can take those matrices and scale the first one up and the second one down by the same factor, or put any invertible matrix in between: multiply the first matrix on the left by some matrix and the other matrix on the right by its inverse. You haven't changed the outputs of the network, but you have changed the weights. So you have many degeneracies like that.

Those are not uninteresting. For example, with the QK matrix, this degeneracy will have an impact on the kinds of functions that part of the network will tend to learn. It's nontrivial, even though on its face it's a bit boring. There are other kinds of degeneracy which emerge in a more overall fashion, which can't be pinned down to individual, obvious forms of degeneracy like that.

items.question: How do you assess the usefulness of toy models for understanding degeneracy in neural networks?
items.object: Toy models for understanding degeneracy in neural networks
items.answer: There is one more kind of theoretical thing you can do: invent toy models of what you think are the key ingredients in a more interesting model. Various papers have looked, for example, at transformers doing in-context learning. You abstract out some of the annoying details in real transformers and come up with a closed-form formula, some function of the parameters that you think models well what transformers are trying to do. Andrew Saxe's lab has made a career out of doing this very beautifully in many different settings, not specifically for transformers. But there's a recent paper which looks at in-context learning for transformers and comes up with a toy model, an explicit potential, some loss function which describes that, and you can see the degeneracy in that function. That's another way of trying to get at it. But if we're talking about algorithms in models and trying to back those out of weights, so far I don't think there's a very clear toy model of that form. It'll be interesting; I don't think it exists yet. So it becomes an empirical question: can you extract signals of that degeneracy from information you get from these empirical losses? The theory says you can do that, and that's a large part of what we do.

items.question: How do you see singular learning theory's connection between weight sensitivity and data sensitivity helping you develop interpretability tools?
items.object: The connection between weight sensitivity and data sensitivity in singular learning theory
items.answer: To come back for a moment to the link between degeneracy and generalization: one of the core theorems of SLT says you can link a sensitivity analysis in weights—the question, if I perturb the weights a little bit, how much does the loss increase?—to a sensitivity analysis in data: if I change the data distribution, how much is my loss going to go up? That link gives us a connection between structure inside the model, reflected in the geometry of the loss landscape, and generalization and potentially out-of-distribution generalization. Now you can look at what happens if I apply a small local change to my data distribution. I upweight some distribution, for example GitHub code data versus WikiText. Which parts of the model become active? Which directions in the loss landscape respond most to this? It's through this connection between structure, geometry, and data that we are developing these tools for interpretability.

items.question: How do you understand the claim that singularities govern the training process of a neural network?
items.object: Singularities as organizing principles of neural network training
items.answer:
There's a bit of mathematical background which I'll provide. Stochastic gradient descent is a specific kind of optimization process. More generally, in many different areas, we're interested in following a gradient. You have some function and then you're going to follow a gradient to maximize it or minimize it. In cases where that gradient is the gradient of something that looks like a sum of squares—x² + y² + z, say—so you're trying to find the bottom of a bowl, that process isn't interesting. There's just the bottom of the bowl; you're going to go there. That's convex optimization. You can still do interesting mathematics with that, but it's fundamentally not a complex process. Many processes in nature do not look like that, and that's why there's a field called nonlinear dynamics.

More generally, if you're trying to follow a potential, imagine a surface covered in little arrows that tell you which direction you're going to go. That's the gradient of some fixed potential. Potential is just a general term for a function whose gradient you're going to follow. You have this vector field, all these arrows pointing various directions. It's a fact about dynamical processes that the places where the gradient vanishes organize the trajectories. In two dimensions, maybe that seems counterintuitive, but in one dimension, take a curve: the places where the gradient vanishes are the maxima, minima, or saddle points. I taught calculus for many years, and a large part of the course is teaching people to classify the minima and maxima, because the other points in the curve are boring. You want to understand a cost function; you want to know where it's maximized or minimized. What it's doing at some random point on the curve is irrelevant. That's an instance of the principle that if you're trying to understand a function, you're often looking for the places where interesting stuff happens. Those are maxima and minima in one dimension; in higher dimensions they're singularities, places where the gradient is zero in all directions.

You can never get there, because no trajectory that starts from outside the singularity ever arrives, and if it's at the singularity it never leaves. But if you follow a random trajectory following a potential and there's a singularity somewhere, it's going to do something around it, and this will dominate the behavior. The trajectories will tend to approach it and then escape in some particular direction. So the singularity is organizing the set of global trajectories. That's an informal statement, but there are formal statements; you can use ideas from topology to make that more precise. That's a general principle, and it applies to learning with SGD just as much as it applies to other systems in physics. That's a general rationale for caring about critical points or singularities. These are almost synonymous. They're the organizing principle for dynamical systems and learning in particular.

What it looks like for an actual learning process in deep learning to be governed by singularities is a complex question. In simple cases, you can see it. In the toy model of superposition I was describing earlier, the columns of the weight matrix can be visualized as vectors in two dimensions. There are two rows of this matrix and some number of columns, and you can plot those columns as vectors. Then you get shapes like a pentagon, a square, or a hexagon. The vertices of those vectors connect, and moving between the neighborhoods of these critical points literally corresponds to growing a leg, contracting a leg, and rearranging the others in some particular way. The growth process of the structure of the network is dictated by the movement between neighborhoods of these different singularities. In a more complex case, it's not so clear how to think about that. These singularities aren't isolated things where there's one singularity here and normal stuff in between. In a large model, there are singularities everywhere. It's not well understood.

items.question: How do you understand what singularities in a neural network's loss landscape represent?
items.object: Singularities in a neural network's loss landscape
items.answer: I think of the singularities as different ways of solving the problem, like different kinds of solutions at a given level of loss. If you're at a given point in the loss landscape, different kinds of singularities correspond to different ways of predicting on the data you've seen so far.

items.question: How do you understand the trade-off between loss and complexity in what singular learning theory calls a type A transition?
items.object: Type A transitions in singular learning theory
items.answer: By trade-off I mean the trade-off between the loss and the complexity as estimated—we call that the LLC, local learning coefficient. I'll just say complexity. One preferred trade-off is to pay the penalty of increasing complexity by lowering the loss. That will decrease what's called the free energy, which determines which solution is more preferred from a Bayesian statistics point of view. That's what we sometimes refer to as a type A transition. That's typical; that's just learning. You learn more stuff, you get better.

items.question: How do you understand grokking in terms of a type B transition, where a model simplifies its algorithm without improving its loss?
items.object: Type B transitions and grokking
items.answer: There is another way to decrease the free energy, which is to decrease the complexity at a fixed loss. This is what we refer to as a type B transition. It's hard to ascertain exactly the conditions under which this is the case, but grokking seems to be one of them. We've seen others. Those are situations where the model really isn't improving on the loss, but it simplifies the algorithm that it's using. We can see this in the linear-regression setting in some sense as well, and there are many other examples of grokking-like behavior. The underlying principle is you should decrease the free energy, which is a sum of two terms: one to do with the loss and one to do with the learning coefficient. You're allowed to increase one of those terms if you decrease the other one enough; that will decrease the free energy. That's normal learning. Then there are situations where you can have a similar change, decrease, by just decreasing one of the terms.

items.question: How do you view double descent from the perspective of singular learning theory?
items.object: Double descent and singular learning theory
items.answer: Regarding double descent, there are various kinds: with respect to training samples and with respect to model size. I think nobody has systematically attempted to study double descent with singular learning theory yet. We haven't really tried. Partly because it just doesn't look that mysterious when you approach the problem from the mathematical perspective that we do. It isn't mysterious that models with many parameters can generalize well.

It isn't mysterious that models with many parameters can generalize well.

items.question: How convincing do you find the intuition that large neural networks optimize well because high-dimensional parameter spaces offer paths around obstacles?
items.object: High dimensionality as an explanation for neural-network optimization and generalization
items.answer: I'm not so sure that's really an explanation. I think that's closer to a folk story. I think it's not understood why. Just having a large model with lots of parameters—you can find things that don't optimize well that have lots of parameters and aren't neural networks, or you can get neural networks configured badly and they won't train very well. There remain many mysteries about why large neural networks can find well-performing, well-generalizing solutions. Singular learning theory doesn't resolve all those mysteries, but it does at least give you a mathematical framework from which you're not surprised there can be models with lots of parameters which do well, predict well, and generalize well.

items.question: How do you understand the role of interpretability in establishing whether an AI model is aligned?
items.object: Interpretability and generalization in AI alignment
items.answer: Big picture, we want to end up with a friendly AI. We don't understand enough about what's going on inside the model to currently make any kinds of guarantees that this model is aligned, this model is not aligned. They can exhibit the same behavior in training and then generalize differently when deployed. For me, the basic premise of interpretability is understanding model internals to a sufficient degree that we can disambiguate these two cases and understand generalization. SLT tells us we can look at the geometry of the loss landscape, look at how structure is reflected in this geometry, and start getting at this question. We have this principled link to in-distribution generalization. That's a starting point for developing a theory of out-of-distribution generalization and better understanding what happens in the case of SGD.

items.question: What do you think perturbation analysis can reveal about a language model's internal structure?
items.object: Perturbation analysis as an approach to model interpretability
items.answer: On the interpretability side, in practice you can probe a bunch of points in the loss landscape. Apply small perturbations to your model—you know, hit it with a hammer—and see how it responds to that probe, to that small perturbation. This tells you something about what's going on internally. This is the basis for starting to extract information about model internals from geometry. We've been looking at a series of projects and papers where we study small language models, subject them to these perturbations, and then measure things like how much does performance decrease? How much worse does performance get under these perturbations? That tells you about the complexity of the solution the model has learned. How much does performance increase if I apply these structured perturbations to a specific part of the model, an attention head or a component? It turns out this can tell you something about whether this attention head is specialized to this kind of data, whether these attention heads are all induction heads, and whether others are doing something else, like memorizing different engrams and skip-engrams. You can start to tear apart the internals of the model using these probes. More recently, we've been looking at applications for circuit discovery. In a principled way, can you associate the components of the model with patterns in data and attribute what structures the model ends up with to the data that activates that structure? This is starting to get the kind of understanding that could lead to an understanding of why the model exhibits the behavior it does, rooted in its internal structures without necessarily having a full mechanistic understanding of what's going on. You can do the sensitivity analysis and it can tell you that these components are involved without needing to know exactly, causally, what the input-to-output map was. So this is more like a top-down approach to interpretability informed through this perturbation analysis.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between reward hacking and overgeneralization toward simpler solutions?
items.object: Reward hacking and overgeneralization
items.answer: The technical way people introduce reward hacking is simply to say that it has found a way of getting more reward than the solution you intended. That's purely about the reward, which is somewhat analogous to the loss. That's not really about complexity; that's about getting more of the explicit target of the optimization process. Under that definition, the answer is no. Reward hacking is not an instance of this trade-off we were referring to earlier, which you're terming overgeneralization. However, it could very well be that instances we currently refer to as reward hacking are partly a trade-off in favor of a simpler solution rather than the one we intended. I don't claim to have evidence for that, but I would hypothesize it.

items.question: Why do you think a model's preference for simpler solutions could create an AI safety risk?
items.object: Simplicity bias as a source of AI safety risk
items.answer:
I think you're referring to one of our hypotheses for how dangerous behavior could arise, somewhat different from the usual story of dangerous behavior arising from overoptimizing a reward target. To go back briefly to the experiments Jesse was referring to earlier: there was a simpler solution, ridge regression. In theory, if you train long enough, you should always switch to memorizing the data because the optimization pressure wants you to get the lowest loss possible. The lowest loss possible is to memorize the data if you can. Typically, training your GPT model, you just can't memorize the data, so you have to generalize. If you can memorize, that's the best thing to do given the training signal. But what we see in that experiment is that in many cases the model sticks at the generalizing solution and never switches to the memorizing one. That's a situation in which, if you imagine the loss landscape—let me draw a curve despite my complaints about that earlier—at the very bottom of the loss landscape there's the thing the training data actually specifies as the optimal solution, which in this case you can prove mathematically is to memorize the tasks. But there is a higher-loss, simpler solution which doesn't memorize but does some more general thing, and training can get stuck there forever even though this is the global minimum. I say 'forever' obviously because we didn't train forever, but it seems like it would stay there forever.

This is a heuristic to have, contrary to some normal stories about AI risk: you may not get what you ask for, what you try to specify in the training data. You get a simplification, a heuristic, an approximation, which is not what you intended or expected. That could be good or bad. In AI safety, people mostly have an intuition that the simpler thing will be better. They have an often-told way of thinking about this: if the model becomes a scheming agent, even though you didn't optimize for this, it has structure in its weights to do the task and then needs to tack on additional structure to take over the world. Because that would be more complex than the solution that just does the task, we have a simplicity bias. That's great, because there's strong pressure to remove the additional dangerous stuff. That may be a reasonable way of thinking about it. I think one should have little confidence in this. It's quite an imprecise story, not really grounded mathematically. That may be the case. But here's an opposite story. The simplification could be quite dangerous.

There's a historical example that's really interesting: the Windrush scandal. The UK in the 1940s allowed citizens of the British Empire to come and settle in the UK without much documentation. Many people came, primarily from the Caribbean. In the 1970s, they changed the laws and started insisting that people have documentation of their citizenship to access services. These people who came as part of this program didn't have the relevant documentation, and some were deported and many bad things happened. There was an investigation and scandal in 2018 looking into this. This is a case where the intended policy of the state obviously wasn't to deport people it had let into the country earlier. But when you follow that policy, the way it's actually implemented at the street level is a simplification of the original intent. It's a brute judgment call at the level of the street-level bureaucrat, and that's what this phenomenon is referred to as: street-level bureaucracy. It's a simplification of what the original policy was trying to specify, and it ends up having unintended negative consequences. I think there's a case to be made that in AI safety we should also be concerned about what happens if the behavior we're specifying at great expense by collecting training data ends up being some kind of simplification of the intended target behavior in ways we don't anticipate and that are undesirable.
